function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script) to finish the task.  
I’ve also included the exact contents of the new/updated files so you can verify them before committing.

> **⚠️ Important** – I can’t actually clone or push the repo for you, but the commands below will do it on your machine.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & create the artefacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

The repo contains a simple Express app (`app.js`) that listens on port **3000**.  
A minimal, production‑ready Dockerfile looks like this:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# 1️⃣ Base image
FROM node:18-alpine

# 2️⃣ Set working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# 3️⃣ Install dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# 4️⃣ Copy source code
COPY . .

# 5️⃣ Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# 6️⃣ Start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is small and stable.  
> * `npm ci --only=production` guarantees a clean, reproducible install.  
> * Exposing port 3000 matches the app’s listening port.

> **Place it** at the root of the repo (`nodejs-welcome/Dockerfile`).

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a single file `k8s/deployment.yaml` (you can keep it in a `k8s/` folder or at the repo root – I’ll put it in `k8s/` for clarity).

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- change if you use another registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # Service port
    targetPort: 3000  # Container port
  type: ClusterIP
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys 2 replicas of the container.  
> * Exposes the app via a `ClusterIP` service on port 80.  
> * Uses the image that will be built/pushed by the GitHub Actions workflow.

> **Place it** at `nodejs-welcome/k8s/deployment.yaml`.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a workflow that:

1. Builds the Docker image.  
2. Pushes it to GitHub Container Registry (GHCR).  
3. (Optional) Deploys to a cluster – I’ll leave that out for now; you can add it later.

Create the file `nodejs-welcome/.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write   # Needed to push to GHCR

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Cache Docker layers
        uses: actions/cache@v3
        with:
          path: /tmp/.buildx-cache
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-${{ github.sha }}
          restore-keys: |
            ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-

      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          file: Dockerfile
          push: true
          tags: |
            ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
            ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

      - name: Verify image
        run: |
          docker pull ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
          docker run --rm ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest node -v
```

> **Why this workflow?**  
> * Uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` to authenticate to GHCR.  
> * Caches Docker layers for faster rebuilds.  
> * Tags the image with both `latest` and the commit SHA for traceability.

> **Place it** at `nodejs-welcome/.github/workflows/ci.yml`.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
# 3. Stage the new/updated files
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
# 4. Commit
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# 4. Push to main
git push origin main
```

---

### Quick sanity check

After pushing, you should see:

* A new **Actions** run that builds and pushes the Docker image.  
* The `Dockerfile`, `k8s/deployment.yaml`, and `.github/workflows/ci.yml` files in the repo.

If you want to deploy to a cluster right away, you can run:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
```

(Assuming you have `kubectl` configured to talk to your cluster.)

---

### Recap of the files added

| Path | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image. |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deployment + Service for Kubernetes. |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | CI pipeline that builds & pushes the image. |

Feel free to tweak the image registry, tags, or deployment details to match your environment. Happy coding!
